title: The Labourer and the Snake
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: A Labourer's little son was bitten by a Snake and died of the wound. The father was beside himself with grief, and in his anger against the Snake he caught up an axe and went and stood close to the Snake's hole, and watched for a chance of killing it.

Presently the Snake came out, and the man aimed a blow at it, but only succeeded in cutting off the tip of its tail before it wriggled in again. He then tried to get it to come out a second time, pretending that he wished to make up the quarrel. But the Snake said, "I can never be your friend because of my lost tail, nor you mine because of your lost child."
Injuries are never forgotten in the presence of those who caused them.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what happens to the Labourer's little son?
options: He falls ill from a fever and recovers slowly
He is lost in the woods for several days
He is bitten by a Snake and dies of the wound
He is injured while helping his father work

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Labourer do in his anger against the Snake?
options: He catches up an axe and waits by the Snake's hole
He sets a trap near his own house
He asks his neighbors to help him hunt the Snake
He burns the grass around the Snake's hole

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what happens when the Snake first comes out?
options: The man kills the Snake immediately
The Snake bites the man before he can strike
The Snake escapes without being touched at all
The man's blow only cuts off the tip of its tail

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the man pretend when trying to lure the Snake out again?
options: That he had food to offer the Snake
That he wished to make up the quarrel
That he was leaving the area for good
That another animal was threatening the Snake's hole

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Snake say about becoming the man's friend?
options: That he is willing to forgive the man completely
That he will only be friends if the man apologizes first
That he can never be the man's friend because of his lost tail
That he no longer cares about what happened

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Snake say about the man's ability to be his friend?
options: The man cannot be his friend either, because of his lost child
The man could be his friend if he apologized properly
The man was never truly his enemy in the first place
The man's loss was not as serious as the Snake's own

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the Snake refuse to trust the man's offer of peace?
options: The Snake does not understand what the man is offering
The Snake believes the man is planning another attack regardless
The Snake wants a different kind of apology before agreeing
The injury the man caused is still fresh and cannot simply be set aside by words

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the Snake's reply suggest is true for both sides of the conflict?
options: Only the Snake has any real reason to remain angry
Each has suffered a loss that makes real friendship between them impossible now
Only the man has any real reason to remain angry
Neither side actually lost anything of true importance

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "wriggled" mean in "it wriggled in again"?
options: Jumped suddenly upward
Crawled very slowly and carefully
Moved with a twisting, snake-like motion
Stopped moving entirely

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable, given its closing line?
options: Serious harm done between two parties leaves a lasting mark that easy words cannot erase
Snakes should never be trusted under any circumstances
Revenge always succeeds if attempted quickly enough
Apologies are always effective at repairing broken trust

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does the father feel after his son's death?
options: Calm and accepting
Confused about what happened
Determined to move away
Beside himself with grief

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the man watch for near the Snake's hole?
options: A chance to trap the Snake alive
A chance of killing the Snake
A chance to seal the hole shut
A chance to warn other villagers

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what part of the Snake does the man's blow actually strike?
options: Its head
Its middle body
The tip of its tail
Nothing at all

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why might the Snake see through the man's pretended peace offering?
options: Given what has already happened between them, its motive still seems suspect despite the kind words
The Snake has no way of understanding human speech at all
The man openly admits his true intentions before the Snake responds
The Snake was warned by another animal beforehand

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the Snake's final statement suggest about whether reconciliation is possible here?
options: It suggests that reconciliation is likely if they wait long enough
It suggests that only the man needs to change his attitude
It suggests that the Snake has already forgiven the man privately
It suggests that some losses are too significant for either side to simply move past

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "quarrel" mean in "make up the quarrel"?
options: A formal agreement or contract
A dispute or conflict between two parties
A physical injury or wound
A type of weapon used in a fight

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: A father successfully befriends the Snake that killed his son
A Snake apologizes to the father and is forgiven completely
A grieving father tries to make peace with a Snake he wounded, but it explains that their mutual losses make true friendship impossible
A father gives up trying to kill the Snake without any further conversation
